english.notes:
(i) WORDING FOR PROTESTS AGAINST MILITARY INSTALLATIONS/BASES: When using this offence to charge campaigners in relation to protests against military bases, etc., it is good practice to charge them with disrupting the security activities on the base rather than the military activities (or whatever), thus avoiding a challenge to the legality of that activity.
(ii) Simply occupying the land could only constitute an act intending to intimidate etc., if there was a 'distinct and overt' action separate from the act of trespass (DPP v Barnard and others 1999).
(iii) See also offence wording H2469.
(iv) It is worth noting that in the case of Nelder and Other v DPP 1998, (Independent dated 8.6.98) a Divisional Court decision, it was held that an information alleging a trespass on land and which stated that they had intended to deter, disrupt or obstruct that activity Contrary to section 68 was not bad for duplicity since deterring, disrupting and obstructing were overlapping concepts. There was, accordingly, no need to charge each element separately.

other.powersofarrest: A constable in uniform who reasonably suspects that a person is committing an offence under this section may arrest him without warrant,.
